top_stories.content: The more than 1,900 startups on the The Crunchbase Unicorn Board have a combined valuation of roughly $9 trillion, based on their last reported valuations. But Crunchbase’s new Current Valuation Model, which estimates how private-company values have changed since their last funding rounds, puts that figure closer to $11 trillion. Most unicorns are estimated to have gained value, even as others have lost ground, our analysis shows. Among the biggest potential gainers are AI startups Thinking Machines Lab, whose estimated value has climbed from $12 billion to $40 billion, and Sierra, from nearly $16 billion to $31.5 billion. The majority of companies on the board are valued higher by the Current Valuations model than they were when they last raised funding. Only around 236 companies — roughly 12% of the board — are down by more than $100 million in value compared to their last reported valuations. The valuation model estimates that a select group of 24 companies have gained more than $10 billion in value since their most recent funding rounds. They include Mira Murati’s AI research lab Thinking Machines Lab, which was last valued at $12 billion in its 2025 seed funding but has a current valuation projected at $40 billion. Similarly, Bret Taylor’s customer oriented AI agent builder Sierra was last valued at close to $16 billion in a May 2026 funding round. It is now estimated to be valued at $31.5 billion, per the Crunchbase model. (On Monday, Bloomberg reported that Sierra is raising a new round at a roughly $30 billion valuation.) top_stories.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
top_stories.content: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not (yet?) available as open weights. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin, then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up. Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one: I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4. It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. items.title: Management consulting is not a thin wrapper on intelligence
items.content: By Rod Moshtagi and Sayash Kapoor. Moshtagi is a researcher at the Harvard Kennedy School and was previously a senior associate at PwC. In summer 2026, he was a GovAI fellow advised by Kapoor, and the research for this essay began as part of the fellowship.Many discussions of AI’s economic impact rest on the implicit assumption that most knowledge work is a “thin wrapper” on intelligence. In this view, the main job of a knowledge worker is to process information. Once AI can match the quality of expert responses in a domain, it should be able to take over most of the work in that domain.Management consulting is a compelling example. The visible outputs of consultants, such as research summaries, slide decks, and financial models, primarily comprise processing information, work that AI already excels at. If the main function of a consulting firm is to provide information, AI looks like an existential threat.Many commentators have drawn this conclusion. In 2025, The Free Press warned that “the consulting crash is coming.” An analyst told Axios that consulting firms are “going to run out of work.” In February 2026, the CEO of the AI startup Mercor predicted that “in the coming two years, we’re going to have chatbots that are as good as the best consulting firm.”In this essay, we argue that apocalyptic predictions about consulting misunderstand both the value of consulting firms and how new technologies change the demand for consulting. We analyze different value propositions of consulting with an eye towards how AI affects them, provide a framework for thinking about the impacts of general-purpose technologies (including AI) on consulting, and recommend how consulting firms can adapt to AI. We make three main arguments:Part 1. Apocalyptic predictions about consulting misunderstand what clients pay for.We break down consulting firms’ work into five sources of value. Analysis is the most visible, but clients also pay for judgment, coordination, credibility, and accountab

items.title: Import AI 482: Huawei kernel benchmarks; airborne drone detection; and a national lab's AI science benchmark
items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. Subscribe nowChinese researchers optimize Huawei chips with a kernel improvement benchmark:…AscendGYM will help China do its own form of RSI…Researchers with the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute, a Chinese research organization, have built and released AscendGYM, “a kernel optimization benchmark for Ascend NPUs”. The purpose of AscendGYM is to make it easier to use AI to develop custom kernels for Ascend chips from Huawei - especially important given the export controls that prevent Chinese organizations from acquiring frontier Western semiconductors and forcing them onto Huawei.What AscendGYM does and contains: The goal is for AscendGYM to be the best way to evaluate the efficacy of AI-designed kernels as well as design new ones. The software is meant to help researchers answer this question: “Given a correct kernel implementation, can the specific agent further improve its performance for a target workload within an acceptable budget while preserving correctness?,” they write. “AscendGYM evaluates performance across multiple deployment cases, the best achievable performance for specific shapes and scenarios, and the optimization cost required to obtain these gains. Together, these dimensions characterize cross-case applicability, shape specialization, and optimization efficiency.” The software includes the AscendForge evaluation environment, which provides unified interfaces for “compilation, correctness checking, performance measurement, and feedback”.How well can AI models optimize Ascend chips? In tests, the single best model is Opus 5, followed by GPT-5.6, followed by GLM-5.3. They test out models in Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode; Claude Code yields the best absolute scores, and GLM does well in it, while GPT does well in Codex. items.title: Ladybird's first alpha release
items.content: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS. This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha, which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself! I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool): Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script, thanks Claude): Ladybird (72925) [240 MB] └── Hub (72926) [61 MB] ├── RequestServer (72927) [29 MB] ├── ProcessReaper (72928) [1 MB] ├── Compositor (72930) [123 MB] ├── RequestServer (72953) [36 MB] ├── WebContent (72984) [819 MB] ├── MediaServer (73006) [118 MB] ├── VideoDecoderServer (73007) [20 MB] ├── WebContent (73052) [144 MB] ├── WebContent (73057) [73 MB] ├── WebContent (73073) [166 MB] ├── WebContent (73094) [70 MB] ├── WebContent (73112) [116 MB] ├── RequestServer (73113) [27 MB] └── WebContent (73185) [60 MB] Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site). I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. all_items.title: [AINews] Jensen Is Back! and OpenAI Shows Its Pretraining Curve, joined by Microsoft
all_items.content: Congrats to Sierra on tripling last year’s $10B valuation, and to Z.ai for releasing GLM 5.4, their first looped transformer following Thinking Machine’s much smaller Inkling Mini 2 from last week. However all these are outshone by today’s twin title stories… Jensen Huang is back. Eleven days after announcing his resignation, Nvidia announced his return as CEO, president and member of the Board of Directors. View post on X ↗ The board voted unanimously after more meetings with Jensen on Sunday and said it received input from senior U.S. officials (aka the Treasury Secretary and the President dialing into the board meeting). Colette Kress remains CFO, the independent directors’ investigation continues, and Jensen’s Senate hearing is still due in 8 days. Nvidia also formed a board committee for national security and export control. As Matt Levine points out, with the firing AND the rehiring by this board with involvement from the government, the investigators are now being put in a position of having had the outcome somewhat predetermined for them, because both have demonstrated that they did not need to wait for any further evidence to come to light. OpenAI put its pretraining loss curve on the record. In Perplexity and Intelligence, Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki plotted base-model log-perplexity back to GPT-3.5 (on their internal held-out coding dataset… which has notable caveats): View post on X ↗ Think of it as how surprised the model is by the next token on a held-out dataset. Lower is better. GPT-3.5 was around 0.99 and GPT-4 around 0.91. When OpenAI put a model around 0.76 (GPT6 Astra) to work on open math problems, hundreds of frontier math problems started falling quickly. Pachocki extrapolates that another jump in capabilities could come around 0.68–0.70. This is all in context of pacing the frontier. all_items.title: Most Unicorns Are Worth More Than Their Last Funding-Round Valuations, Crunchbase Estimates
all_items.content: The more than 1,900 startups on the The Crunchbase Unicorn Board have a combined valuation of roughly $9 trillion, based on their last reported valuations. But Crunchbase’s new Current Valuation Model, which estimates how private-company values have changed since their last funding rounds, puts that figure closer to $11 trillion. Most unicorns are estimated to have gained value, even as others have lost ground, our analysis shows. Among the biggest potential gainers are AI startups Thinking Machines Lab, whose estimated value has climbed from $12 billion to $40 billion, and Sierra, from nearly $16 billion to $31.5 billion. The majority of companies on the board are valued higher by the Current Valuations model than they were when they last raised funding. Only around 236 companies — roughly 12% of the board — are down by more than $100 million in value compared to their last reported valuations. The valuation model estimates that a select group of 24 companies have gained more than $10 billion in value since their most recent funding rounds. They include Mira Murati’s AI research lab Thinking Machines Lab, which was last valued at $12 billion in its 2025 seed funding but has a current valuation projected at $40 billion. Similarly, Bret Taylor’s customer oriented AI agent builder Sierra was last valued at close to $16 billion in a May 2026 funding round. It is now estimated to be valued at $31.5 billion, per the Crunchbase model. (On Monday, Bloomberg reported that Sierra is raising a new round at a roughly $30 billion valuation.) Physical Intelligence, a company building AI for robotics, was valued at $5.6 billion in its Series B. Crunchbase’s Current Valuation model estimates its valuation now at $18.5 billion. Another 53 companies are estimated to have current valuations that are $5 billion to just under $10 billion higher than those achieved in their most recent funding rounds. all_items.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
all_items.content: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not (yet?) available as open weights. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin, then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up. Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one: I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4. It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. all_items.title: Management consulting is not a thin wrapper on intelligence
all_items.content: By Rod Moshtagi and Sayash Kapoor. Moshtagi is a researcher at the Harvard Kennedy School and was previously a senior associate at PwC. In summer 2026, he was a GovAI fellow advised by Kapoor, and the research for this essay began as part of the fellowship.Many discussions of AI’s economic impact rest on the implicit assumption that most knowledge work is a “thin wrapper” on intelligence. In this view, the main job of a knowledge worker is to process information. Once AI can match the quality of expert responses in a domain, it should be able to take over most of the work in that domain.Management consulting is a compelling example. The visible outputs of consultants, such as research summaries, slide decks, and financial models, primarily comprise processing information, work that AI already excels at. If the main function of a consulting firm is to provide information, AI looks like an existential threat.Many commentators have drawn this conclusion. In 2025, The Free Press warned that “the consulting crash is coming.” An analyst told Axios that consulting firms are “going to run out of work.” In February 2026, the CEO of the AI startup Mercor predicted that “in the coming two years, we’re going to have chatbots that are as good as the best consulting firm.”In this essay, we argue that apocalyptic predictions about consulting misunderstand both the value of consulting firms and how new technologies change the demand for consulting. We analyze different value propositions of consulting with an eye towards how AI affects them, provide a framework for thinking about the impacts of general-purpose technologies (including AI) on consulting, and recommend how consulting firms can adapt to AI. We make three main arguments:Part 1. Apocalyptic predictions about consulting misunderstand what clients pay for.We break down consulting firms’ work into five sources of value. all_items.title: Import AI 482: Huawei kernel benchmarks; airborne drone detection; and a national lab's AI science benchmark
all_items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. Subscribe nowChinese researchers optimize Huawei chips with a kernel improvement benchmark:…AscendGYM will help China do its own form of RSI…Researchers with the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute, a Chinese research organization, have built and released AscendGYM, “a kernel optimization benchmark for Ascend NPUs”. The purpose of AscendGYM is to make it easier to use AI to develop custom kernels for Ascend chips from Huawei - especially important given the export controls that prevent Chinese organizations from acquiring frontier Western semiconductors and forcing them onto Huawei.What AscendGYM does and contains: The goal is for AscendGYM to be the best way to evaluate the efficacy of AI-designed kernels as well as design new ones. The software is meant to help researchers answer this question: “Given a correct kernel implementation, can the specific agent further improve its performance for a target workload within an acceptable budget while preserving correctness?,” they write. “AscendGYM evaluates performance across multiple deployment cases, the best achievable performance for specific shapes and scenarios, and the optimization cost required to obtain these gains. Together, these dimensions characterize cross-case applicability, shape specialization, and optimization efficiency.” The software includes the AscendForge evaluation environment, which provides unified interfaces for “compilation, correctness checking, performance measurement, and feedback”.How well can AI models optimize Ascend chips? In tests, the single best model is Opus 5, followed by GPT-5.6, followed by GLM-5.3. They test out models in Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode; Claude Code yields the best absolute scores, and GLM does well in it, while GPT does well in Codex. Here's a demo video, recorded on agent.datasette.io where you can sign in with GitHub to try the plugin yourself: Download the video (MP4) I prompt Datasette Agent to "Use #stats to show sqlite-utils downloads over time as a chart" - where typing "#stats" opens a table search box. It shows me a chart inline in the chat, and when I click "Open in the chart builder" it opens the chart in a panel along with the table page. I use the table page to switch to a chart of "datasette", then when I ask the agent "what does the chart show?" it notices that I changed the content in the panel and describes the new Datasette chart to me. Here's a Markdown export of the chat from the video. Tags: datasette-agent, datasette, visualization

all_items.title: Ladybird's first alpha release
all_items.content: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS. This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha, which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself! I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool): Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script, thanks Claude): Ladybird (72925) [240 MB] └── Hub (72926) [61 MB] ├── RequestServer (72927) [29 MB] ├── ProcessReaper (72928) [1 MB] ├── Compositor (72930) [123 MB] ├── RequestServer (72953) [36 MB] ├── WebContent (72984) [819 MB] ├── MediaServer (73006) [118 MB] ├── VideoDecoderServer (73007) [20 MB] ├── WebContent (73052) [144 MB] ├── WebContent (73057) [73 MB] ├── WebContent (73073) [166 MB] ├── WebContent (73094) [70 MB] ├── WebContent (73112) [116 MB] ├── RequestServer (73113) [27 MB] └── WebContent (73185) [60 MB] Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site). I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly.
